pr.title: Run CI on the release pull request the Release workflow opens
pr.head: b294214535eaf143023a5729a39ea2c3bc8c7cbd

summary: Field releases through a GitHub Actions workflow, .github/workflows/release.yml. You start it by hand, its propose job raises the version in package.json on a release/vX.Y.Z branch and opens a pull request, and merging that pull request is the decision to ship. The workflow opens the pull request with GITHUB_TOKEN, the token GitHub gives every workflow run.

The first release pull request, #207, showed no checks when it opened. This change makes CI start on every release pull request by itself: after the propose job opens the pull request, or finds one already open on a re-run, it runs gh workflow run ci.yml --ref release/vX.Y.Z. That starts a workflow_dispatch run of CI on the release branch, so ci.yml gains workflow_dispatch as a trigger, and the propose job gains actions: write, the permission a dispatch needs.

The change also documents the three levels at which an administrator must let Actions open pull requests (enterprise, organization, and repository), which the first release run ran into, and it updates the release pull request's own Testing text. The plan, docs/projects/install/readme.md §9.1, records both.

Read the review's open finding before anything else. The change rests on GitHub starting no workflow for a pull request that GITHUB_TOKEN opened. GitHub's documentation and #207's own CI run say otherwise: GitHub creates those runs held for approval, and a maintainer starts them with Approve workflows to run.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• GITHUB_TOKEN: the token GitHub gives each workflow run. Events it causes mostly start no further workflows.
  • workflow_dispatch: the event that starts a workflow on request, from the Actions tab or gh workflow run. A GITHUB_TOKEN dispatch still starts a run.
  • Held run: a pull_request run GitHub creates in an approval-required state, shown as action_required, until someone with write access approves it.
  • Propose job: the Release workflow job that bumps the version and opens the release pull request.

cards.title: What happened on #206 and #207
cards.html:
• Release run 38167355504 failed its first attempt, because the enterprise did not let Actions open pull requests.
  • #206 was opened by hand from the pushed branch and closed a minute later. Its CI ran normally.
  • A re-run of the Release workflow opened #207 as github-actions[bot]. CI run 38167745651 was created four seconds later and ended action_required. A maintainer started its second attempt 22 seconds after that, and linux passed.
  • #207 merged at 19:25:19Z, and Release run 38167947880 tagged and released v0.2.0.

groups.title: The release dispatches CI
groups.kicker: The propose job starts CI on the release branch, and CI accepts the dispatch.
intro: A workflow run cannot normally start another one: GitHub ignores most events that GITHUB_TOKEN causes, to keep workflows from triggering each other in a loop. A dispatch is one of the exceptions. So the propose job ends with gh workflow run ci.yml --ref "$branch", on both of its paths: after it opens the pull request, and after it finds one already open on a re-run.

A dispatched run tests the tip of the release branch, which is the pull request's head commit, and GitHub records its checks on that commit. Because the dispatch reads ci.yml from the release branch, and that branch starts from main, it works only once this change is on main.

checks.text: CI's concurrency group is CI- plus github.ref. A dispatched run's ref is refs/heads/release/vX.Y.Z, and a pull_request run's is refs/pull/<n>/merge, so a dispatched run cancels an older dispatched run on the same branch but never a pull_request run.

files.note: Adds workflow_dispatch to the triggers, with a comment giving the reason.

checks.text: No job or step in ci.yml reads github.event_name or github.event.pull_request, so both jobs run the same steps under a dispatch. Checked by parsing the file and reading every job.
Repeats the claim from the open finding on docs/release.md: GitHub holds the release pull request's run for approval rather than starting none, and workflow_dispatch is not the only exception.

files.note: The propose job gains actions: write and ends with the dispatch. The release pull request body now says CI was dispatched and describes released --since.

checks.text: actions: write is scoped to the propose job, which runs only on workflow_dispatch. The publish job keeps the top-level contents: write, and the repository default token permission is still read, read with gh api repos/okamnesiac/field/actions/permissions/workflow.
The heredoc renders cleanly with stand-in values: every backtick is escaped, and only $version and $BUMP expand. Rendered locally from the parsed step.

No ${{ }} expression appears inside a run step. $branch comes from the version that scripts/release.ts bump prints, and it is quoted. Under set -euo pipefail, a failed dispatch fails the job after the pull request is open, and a re-run dispatches again.
Repeats the claim from the open finding on docs/release.md. The held pull_request run still appears beside the dispatched run.

groups.title: The release guide and the plan
groups.kicker: Why CI is dispatched, the three settings levels, and the plan record.
intro: docs/release.md is the guide to cutting a release. It now says that the workflow starts CI on the release pull request and why, and it names the three levels of Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests: the enterprise, the organization, and the repository. Each level must allow it before the one below can.

The install plan's §9.1, "What implementation settled" for chunk 2, records the enterprise policy that stopped the first release run, and the dispatch with the GitHub App token it beat. The plan stays in-progress.

files.note: Step 2 now says the workflow starts CI. A new paragraph explains the dispatch, and the settings paragraph names all three levels.

checks.text: Open review finding: GitHub does not skip CI for a pull request that GITHUB_TOKEN opens. It creates the pull_request run held for approval, and the merge box offers Approve workflows to run, which is what #207 got. repository_dispatch is also exempt, so "the one event" is wrong too. Approving the held run beside the dispatched one runs linux and windows twice, because their concurrency groups differ.

files.note: §9.1 replaces the repository-setting bullet with the enterprise policy, and adds the dispatch decision.

checks.text: Records the same claim as the open finding, and names the GitHub App token as the alternative the dispatch beat. It does not record the cheaper alternative, approving the held run, which is what #207 used.

Run 38167355504 is real: its first attempt failed, and its second attempt opened #207. §9.2 still says the workflow has not run, and §9.3 still owes the first release, which shipped as v0.2.0. Those lines predate this change.
